title: How American musicians tour Europe and local rhythm sections
summary: Musicians go club to club and are treated well; local players are good, though audiences vary.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Yeah, well, that's been one of the patterns for the -- one of the ways in which American jazz musicians have toured the country. They'd go from club to club and play with the local --

It's very good, you know, it's very good because like I said it was not easy to take a band over, but individual musicians can go over there and appear all over the Continent and the British Isles and one of the advantages there, one of the arrangements that is very good on tour like that as individual musicians, you don't get involved in staying in hotels. Everybody is quite happy and

willing to have you stay with them, you know, so you're big thing is getting there, that's half the battle and once you're there you're treated royally, they roll out the carpet, and there are a lot of good musicians over there, you know --
Increasingly the local rhythm section is in fact likely to be an American-born rhythm section.
Well, it's more the case now than it was.

I found -- I heard some very good musicians over there but I visited some of the little jazz clubs and there was a club in Stockholm, they had a six-piece band there, a Dixieland combination and the trumpet player was so much like Billy Butterfield it wasn't even funny and they were playing very good jazz. But, I talked with the leader and he said all the guys in the group came from different sections of the country and then maybe they'd have one gig in four months and they would travel as far as like 400 miles to get to the gig. So although we experi-
